record.original_question: Let K_0, K_1, K_2, K_3, S, M, and G be the classes of groups considered in the paper, and recall that Theorem 1.1 proves the following statement whenever A and B are members of this collection with B properly contained in A and A containing K_3: there is no algorithm that decides, given a finite presentation of a group known to lie in A, whether that group lies in B. Does the same undecidability statement remain true in the case A = K_2?

evidence.quote: Theorem 1.1. Let A and B be members of {K0, K1, K2, K3, S,M, G} such that B ( A and A ⊃ K3. Then there does not exist an algorithm that can decide, given a finite presentation of a group G in A whether or not G is in B.
We conjecture that Theorem 1.1 also holds for A = K2; we show that this is true if there is a group in K2 with unsolvable word problem.

artifact.status_search_result: The conjecture was left open in the original work, where it was shown to follow from the existence of a 2-knot group with unsolvable word problem. Web searches indicate that whether any 2-knot group has unsolvable word problem remains an open question; no resolution of the K_2 case has been reported.

status_evidence.title: Unsolvable problems about higher-dimensional knots and related groups
status_evidence.snippet: We conjecture that Theorem 1.1 also holds for A=K_2; we show that this is true if there is a group in K_2 with unsolvable word problem.
status_evidence.claim: The K_2 case is conjectural and reduces to the existence of a 2-knot group with unsolvable word problem.

status_evidence.title: The Word Problem for Groups and Applications to Knot Theory
status_evidence.snippet: if there is a group with unsolvable word problem in dimension n, then it is impossible to find a procedure for n-knots ... we do not know if such groups exist in dimension 2.
status_evidence.claim: It is unknown whether 2-knot groups with unsolvable word problem exist.
